title: SIM Swap Scam: Signs, What to Do and How to Protect Your Number
html:
In a SIM swap scam, a fraudster gets your phone number moved onto a SIM they control. Then the OTPs and calls meant for you go to them. The first sign is often that your phone suddenly shows no signal while Wi-Fi still works. If that happens, contact your mobile operator and your bank at once, from another phone.

Last updated: 10 Oct 2026. Operators' procedures differ; check yours.

Sources last checked: 10 Oct 2026.

Signs to watch for

  • Your phone suddenly shows "No service" or "Emergency calls only", while Wi-Fi works.
  • Calls and texts stop arriving, or friends say your number is switched off.
  • You get a message from your operator about a SIM change or an eSIM activation that you did not ask for.
  • You get alerts from your bank, email or social accounts about sign-ins or password changes you did not make.

Any one of these can have other causes, such as a network fault. Do not wait to find out if you also see account alerts.

What to do in the first minutes

  1. Call your operator from another phone and ask whether a SIM replacement or eSIM activation was done on your number. Ask them to block the new SIM and reissue yours.
  2. Call your bank on its official number and ask them to block UPI, cards and net banking until the number is back with you.
  3. Change the passwords for your email and bank logins, starting with the email, using a different device. See our Google account checklist.
  4. If money has moved, report it on the cybercrime helpline 1930 or at cybercrime.gov.in, as Sanchar Saathi advises. The steps are in our fraud reporting guide.

Check the connections in your name

Sanchar Saathi has a service to check how many mobile connections are registered in your name (TAFCOP). The portal says you log in with an OTP on your registered number, review your active connections, and report any that are not yours or that you no longer need. Do this once now, and after any SIM scare.

The seven-day rule for porting codes

TRAI's amended Mobile Number Portability regulations took effect on 1 July 2024. Under them, a Unique Porting Code (UPC) is not allocated if the request is made before the expiry of seven days after a SIM swap or replacement.

Protect your number

  • Never share a code or ID. The RBI says not to share your password, PIN, OTP, CVV or UPI PIN with anyone, and that banks never ask for them. The same goes for any OTP you get about a SIM change or eSIM activation.
  • Keep your documents private. Do not send photos of your ID or SIM details to anyone who contacts you.
  • Do not rely on SMS for your most important accounts. Use an authenticator app or a passkey. See our two-factor authentication guide.
  • Ask your operator what protection it offers against SIM changes, and what proof it asks for before replacing a SIM.
  • Turn on bank and email alerts so you hear about a change quickly.

What to do next

  1. Check your connections on Sanchar Saathi today.
  2. Switch your email, bank and payment accounts from SMS codes to an authenticator app or passkey.
  3. Save your operator's and your bank's official numbers, so you can call them from another phone.
